so101_base_m1_insert.requirements:
Context: This is the first assembly step of building an SO-101 robot arm from loose parts with two robot arms on a plain table. The Base is the arm's foundation and M1 is the servo motor that becomes the arm's first joint (shoulder pan); later steps mount further parts on M1, so M1 must sit exactly at its designed pose in Base.
Goal: Assemble the orange servo motor (M1) into the blue Base exactly as in the CAD assembly in /work/cad.
Completion: M1 reaches its CAD assembled pose relative to Base and is fully seated: the next step's retaining cap only fits over an M1 that is pushed all the way to its designed depth, so stopping a fraction of a millimetre short makes the next step impossible. The station stands in for the screws: after every finished action it checks whether M1 is physically seated within tolerance and, if so, fastens it. Each observation reports this as `station.fastened`. Once it is true M1 is rigidly joined to Base: release M1 and withdraw both hands; do not pull or push it further.
Process rules: Base stays on the table and is never lifted; during insertion one hand holds Base against the table. Use only the two grippers and the table; no other supports.
Required strategy: /work/cad holds the design meshes of Base and M1 in their body frames and the assembled pose of M1 in Base. Use the CAD to: (1) recognise each part and its features in the images and estimate each part's body-frame pose on the table; (2) work out, from the mating geometry, how M1 can enter Base: the free approach and the insertion direction and depth that end at the assembled pose; (3) choose grip regions on Base and on M1 that stay clear of that path and of the mating surfaces, and that let one hand hold Base on the table while the other carries M1; (4) turn the estimated part poses and the assembled pose into concrete gripper targets. Decide this before moving; do not search for the fit by trial-and-error contact.
Optional considerations: Re-estimate part poses from fresh images after each contact action, since grasping or holding can shift a part.
Experience: /work/experience.md is the station's record of earlier episodes of this task on this robot: measured arm reach, which targets the planner rejected, how earlier attempts ended according to the evaluator, and the policy's own last summary from those episodes. Each episode starts with empty memory, so read that file before the first plan and carry its lessons into `memory`.
Skills: /work/skills/INDEX.md lists reusable procedures distilled from earlier episodes on this robot (reach, holding the Base, pushing a part to its seat, releasing after fastening, ...), one line each; open the ones that apply before planning.
so101_base_m1_insert.finish: Finish: Return both arms to their supplied initial positions and orientations after completing the task.

so101_m1_cap_install.requirements:
Context: This is the second assembly step of building an SO-101 robot arm from loose parts with two robot arms on a plain table. In the first step M1, the servo that becomes the arm's first joint, was seated in the Base and fastened. Now the green retaining cap goes over M1 into the Base; it clamps M1 in its seat and later carries the shoulder parts, so it must reach its designed pose exactly.
Goal: Install the green retaining cap on the Base+M1 assembly exactly as in the CAD assembly in /work/cad.
Completion: The cap reaches its CAD assembled pose relative to Base, and M1 stays at its assembled pose. The station stands in for the screws: after every finished action it checks whether the cap is physically seated within tolerance and, if so, fastens it. Process rules: The Base+M1 assembly stays on the table and is never lifted; during installation one hand holds it against the table. Do not push M1 out of its seat. Use only the two grippers and the table; no other supports.
Required strategy: /work/cad holds the design meshes of Base, M1 and the cap in their body frames and the assembled poses of M1 and the cap in the Base frame. Use the CAD to: (1) recognise the parts and their features in the images and estimate the body-frame poses of the cap and of the Base+M1 assembly; (2) work out, from the mating geometry of the cap with Base and M1, how the cap reaches its assembled pose: the free approach, the final direction and the depth; (3) choose grip regions on the cap and on the Base+M1 assembly that stay clear of that path and of the mating surfaces, so one hand holds the assembly on the table while the other carries the cap; (4) turn the estimated poses and the assembled pose into concrete gripper targets. Decide this before moving; do not search for the fit by trial-and-error contact.
Optional considerations: Re-estimate part poses from fresh images after each contact action, since grasping or holding can shift a part.

so101_shoulder_fork_install.requirements:
Context: This is the third assembly step of building an SO-101 robot arm from loose parts with two robot arms on a plain table. Steps 1 and 2 seated the servo M1 in the Base and fastened the retaining cap over it. M1's output (its two round horns, one above and one below the servo) is the arm's first joint, shoulder pan. Now the yellow shoulder fork is mounted on those horns; everything above the base hangs from it, so it must reach its designed pose exactly.
Goal: Mount the yellow shoulder fork on M1's output horns exactly as in the CAD assembly in /work/cad.
Completion: The fork reaches its CAD assembled pose relative to M1's output, and M1 and the cap stay at their assembled poses. The station stands in for the screws: after every finished action it checks whether the fork is physically seated within tolerance and, if so, fastens it to the horns. Each observation reports this as `station.fastened`. Once it is true the fork is rigidly joined to the M1 output: release the fork and withdraw both hands; do not pull or push it further.
Process rules: The Base assembly stays on the table and is never lifted; during installation one hand holds it against the table. Do not push M1 or the cap out of their seats. Use only the two grippers and the table; no other supports.
Required strategy: /work/cad holds the design meshes of Base, M1, the cap and the fork in their body frames and their assembled poses in the Base frame. Use the CAD to: (1) recognise the parts and their features in the images and estimate the body-frame poses of the fork and of the Base assembly; (2) work out, from the mating geometry of the fork with M1's horns, the Base and the cap, how the fork reaches its assembled pose: the free approach, the final direction and the depth; (3) choose grip regions on the fork and on the Base assembly that stay clear of that path and of the mating surfaces, so one hand holds the assembly on the table while the other carries the fork; (4) turn the estimated poses and the assembled pose into concrete gripper targets. Decide this before moving; do not search for the fit by trial-and-error contact.
Optional considerations: Re-estimate part poses from fresh images after each contact action, since grasping or holding can shift a part. The Base assembly may be slid or turned on the table if that makes the approach reachable; it must not leave the table.
